sources.artifact_title: Address to the Weimar National Assembly by Reich President Friedrich Ebert
sources.creator: Friedrich Ebert (Reich President of the Weimar Republic)
sources.repository: German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv), Berlin / Reichstag Protocols
sources.accession_id: Verhandlungen der verfassunggebenden Deutschen Nationalversammlung, Vol. 326
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official Government Speech Delivered 1919 — CDPA 1988 / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: Reich President Friedrich Ebert delivering the keynote opening address to the newly elected Weimar National Assembly on 6 February 1919.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Friedrich Ebert emphasise both lawful democratic order at home and resistance to Allied vengeance abroad in his opening address?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Territorial Losses under the Treaty of Versailles (1919)
sources.creator: Allied Peace Commission / German Cartographic Institute
sources.repository: National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) / Imperial War Museum
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Cartography)
sources.caption: Versailles Territorial Losses (1919): Germany surrendered 13% of its European territory, including Alsace-Lorraine and the Polish Corridor, separating East Prussia from the German mainland.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the geographic division of East Prussia by the Polish Corridor particularly humiliating to the German military establishment?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Children Playing with Banknote Bricks during Hyperinflation
sources.creator: German Press Agency Photojournalist
sources.repository: German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv), Koblenz
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: The Hyperinflation Catastrophe (1923): Money lost its value so rapidly that millions of marks were bundled into bricks for children's games, permanently wiping out middle-class life savings.
sources.hinge_question: How did hyperinflation permanently destroy the Weimar middle class's faith in democratic governance, even after the currency was stabilized?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: The "Stab in the Back" (Dolchstoßlegende) Nationalist Postcard
sources.creator: Austrian Nationalist Publisher
sources.repository: Austrian National Library (ÖNB) / Imperial War Museum
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Published Propaganda)
sources.caption: Austrian and German right-wing postcard depicting the "Stab in the Back" (Dolchstoßlegende), claiming German frontline soldiers were betrayed from behind by socialist and Jewish home-front politicians.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the "Stab in the Back" myth so politically toxic for the long-term legitimacy of the Weimar democracy?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Marinebrigade Ehrhardt Freikorps during the Kapp Putsch
sources.creator: Berlin Press Agency Photojournalist
sources.repository: German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv), Koblenz
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: Mutinous soldiers of the Ehrhardt Naval Brigade wearing swastika-painted steel helmets occupying the government district in Berlin during the right-wing Kapp Putsch.
sources.hinge_question: Why did General von Seeckt declare that "Reichswehr does not fire on Reichswehr" when the Weimar government ordered the military to crush the Kapp Putsch?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: One-Trillion-Mark Banknote Issued by the Reichsbank
sources.creator: Reichsbank Directorate, Berlin
sources.repository: German Federal Archives Numismatic Collection
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official German State Banknote / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: Official 1,000,000,000,000 Mark banknote printed only on one side by the Reichsbank in Berlin during the astronomical monetary collapse of November 1923.
sources.hinge_question: Why did hyperinflation inflict far greater psychological trauma on the German middle class than on industrial tycoons who owned physical assets?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Eyewitness Account of the 1923 Hyperinflation by Erna von Pustau
sources.creator: Erna von Pustau (Hamburg Citizen and Eyewitness)
sources.repository: Hamburg State Archives / Contemporary Published Account
sources.accession_id: Erna von Pustau & Pearl S. Buck, The Way to Poverty (1923)
sources.rights_status: Educational Quotation / Public Domain (Historical Memoir Extract 1923 — Section 30 CDPA 1988)
sources.caption: Eyewitness diary account written by Erna von Pustau, recording the daily panic and social humiliation of hyperinflation in Hamburg in late 1923.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the 1923 hyperinflation destroy middle-class trust in parliamentary democracy far more deeply than the military defeat of 1918?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.2: Early Challenges to the Republic, 1919–1923
sources.artifact_title: Revolutionary Soldiers at the Brandenburg Gate (Spartacist Uprising)
sources.creator: German Press Agency Photojournalist
sources.repository: German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv), Berlin
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Official Photograph)
sources.caption: Armed revolutionary troops occupying positions around the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin during the communist Spartacist Uprising led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht.
sources.hinge_question: Why did the brutal suppression of the Spartacist Uprising create a permanent, irreconcilable hatred between the SPD and the Communist Party (KPD)?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The 1-Rentenmark Banknote Halting Hyperinflation
sources.creator: Deutsche Rentenbank, Berlin
sources.repository: German Federal Archives (Bundesarchiv) Numismatic Collection
sources.accession_id: Deutsche Rentenbank Berlin Serie A / 1 Rentenmark
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Official German State Banknote / Section 5 UrhG)
sources.caption: The Rentenmark Miracle (November 1923): Backed by agricultural mortgages and industrial assets, Gustav Stresemann's new currency abruptly restored public confidence and halted hyperinflation.
sources.hinge_question: Why was a psychological anchor—backing currency with industrial real estate rather than scarce gold—sufficient to restore public faith in the German currency?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Gustav Stresemann Addressing the League of Nations in Geneva
sources.creator: Photopress / Keystone Geneva
sources.repository: United Nations Archives Geneva (UNOG) / Bundesarchiv
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Historical Public Domain
sources.caption: Germany Enters the League of Nations (September 1926): Foreign Minister Stresemann delivered Germany's maiden address in Geneva, securing a permanent seat on the League Council as an equal great power.
sources.hinge_question: How did Germany's permanent Council seat in the League of Nations undermine right-wing claims that Weimar politicians were merely passive puppets of the victorious Allies?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Gustav Stresemann and European Foreign Ministers at Locarno
sources.creator: Swiss Press Agency / Keystone Press
sources.repository: Swiss National Library, Bern
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Historical Archive Record
sources.caption: German Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann with French Foreign Minister Aristide Briand and British Foreign Secretary Austen Chamberlain at Locarno, guaranteeing Germany's western borders.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Stresemann agree to guarantee Germany's western borders with France and Belgium while refusing to give similar guarantees for its eastern borders with Poland and Czechoslovakia?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: $1,000 Gold Bond Certificate for the Dawes Loan
sources.creator: German External Loan 1924 / J.P. Morgan & Co.
sources.repository: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Historical Archives
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Pre-1925 Published Financial Security)
sources.caption: Official 7% Gold Bond certificate for $1,000 issued by the German government under the Dawes Plan, floated by J.P. Morgan & Co. in New York to finance German economic recovery.
sources.hinge_question: How did the Dawes Plan create a dangerous economic cycle where Germany relied entirely on American loans to pay British and French reparations?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The Signing of the Kellogg-Briand Pact in Paris
sources.creator: French Foreign Ministry / Library of Congress
sources.repository: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division, Washington D.C.
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & US Gov Archive Record
sources.caption: Representatives of 15 world powers, including German Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann, signing the Kellogg-Briand Pact in Paris renouncing war as an instrument of national policy.
sources.hinge_question: Why did German nationalist parties fiercely denounce Stresemann for signing the Kellogg-Briand Pact when it offered moral protection against foreign invasion?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Nationalist Anti-Young Plan Campaign Poster (Herbert Rothgaengel)
sources.creator: Herbert Rothgaengel / Reichsausschuss für das deutsche Volksbegehren
sources.repository: Deutsches Historisches Museum (DHM), Berlin
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Historical Political Poster
sources.caption: Right-wing propaganda poster by Herbert Rothgaengel for the 1929 "Freedom Law" referendum, claiming the Young Plan would enslave German children to pay reparations until 1988.
sources.hinge_question: How did the national campaign against the Young Plan in 1929 allow Adolf Hitler to gain nationwide mainstream political respectability and media coverage?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.3: The Recovery of the Republic, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Confidential Foreign Policy Letter to Crown Prince Wilhelm by Gustav Stresemann
sources.creator: Gustav Stresemann (Foreign Minister of the Weimar Republic)
sources.repository: Political Archive of the Federal Foreign Office (Politisches Archiv des Auswärtigen Amts), Berlin
sources.accession_id: PA AA, Nachlass Gustav Stresemann, Bd. 311
sources.rights_status: Public Domain (Historical Diplomatic Correspondence 1925 — CDPA 1988)
sources.caption: Confidential letter written by Weimar Foreign Minister Gustav Stresemann to the exiled Crown Prince Wilhelm on 7 September 1925, explaining his diplomatic strategy.
sources.hinge_question: Does Source E prove that Stresemann was a cynical nationalist pretending to be a European peacemaker, or a realistic statesman protecting Germany's vital national interests?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The "New Woman" of the Golden Twenties in Berlin
sources.creator: Ullstein Bild / Berlin Fashion Photographer
sources.repository: Ullstein Bilderdienst / German Federal Archives, Berlin
sources.accession_id: Ullstein Bild No. 00024951 / Berlin Neue Frau c. 1926
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Archival Record
sources.caption: The "New Woman" (Neue Frau) in 1920s Berlin: Benefiting from constitutional equality under Article 109, young women embraced financial independence, shorter skirts, and modern clerical employment.
sources.hinge_question: To what extent did the "New Woman" represent a nationwide social revolution, rather than a phenomenon limited to young middle-class women in major cities?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The Bauhaus Architectural Complex in Dessau
sources.creator: Walter Gropius (Architect) / Bauhaus Archive
sources.repository: Bauhaus-Archiv Museum für Gestaltung, Berlin
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Architectural Record
sources.caption: The Bauhaus at Dessau (1925–1926): Walter Gropius revolutionized architecture by pioneering functional glass-curtain walls, clean steel geometries, and the principle that "form follows function".
sources.hinge_question: Why did modernist institutions like the Bauhaus provoke intense hatred from right-wing traditionalists who viewed internationalist art as "degenerate" (entartet)?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Otto Dix, The Skat Players (Card-Playing War Cripples, 1920)
sources.creator: Otto Dix (1891–1969)
sources.repository: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin, Neue Nationalgalerie
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 (Criticism & Review)
sources.caption: Otto Dix's famous Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity) painting depicting three severely mutilated Great War veterans playing cards using prosthetic limbs and facial grafts.
sources.hinge_question: How did expressionist artists like Otto Dix challenge both romantic imperial militarism and the superficial consumerism of the Weimar "Golden Twenties"?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Contemporary Analysis of the "New Woman" (Die neue Frau) by Alice Rühle-Gerstel
sources.creator: Alice Rühle-Gerstel (German Psychologist and Social Commentator)
sources.repository: German National Library (Deutsche Nationalbibliothek), Leipzig / Die literarische Welt
sources.accession_id: Die literarische Welt, Berlin, Vol. 3, No. 39 (1927)
sources.rights_status: Public Domain / Educational Fair Dealing (Published 1927 — CDPA 1988 / Section 30)
sources.caption: Contemporary essay by social commentator Alice Rühle-Gerstel in Die literarische Welt (1927), analysing the real versus superficial emancipation of German women.
sources.hinge_question: Why was the social freedom of the "New Woman" celebrated as a triumph of Weimar democracy by urban liberals, while being fiercely condemned as moral degeneracy by rural conservatives?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Theatrical Release Poster for Fritz Lang's Metropolis (UFA Studios, 1927)
sources.creator: Heinz Schulz-Neudamm / Universum Film AG (UFA)
sources.repository: Deutsche Kinemathek – Museum für Film und Fernsehen, Berlin
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Historical Movie Poster
sources.caption: Official German release poster for Fritz Lang's dystopian science-fiction film Metropolis, produced by UFA Studios in Babelsberg, illustrating Germany's pioneering cinematic dominance.
sources.hinge_question: How did Fritz Lang's Metropolis reflect Weimar Germany's deep anxiety over industrial modernization, mass mechanization, and class conflict?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: The Horseshoe Estate (Hufeisensiedlung) in Berlin-Britz
sources.creator: Bruno Taut & Martin Wagner (Architects)
sources.repository: Landesarchiv Berlin / UNESCO World Heritage Archive
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Architectural Record
sources.caption: The Horseshoe Estate in Berlin-Britz, constructed between 1925 and 1930 by socialist architect Bruno Taut to provide affordable, sunlit municipal housing for working-class families.
sources.hinge_question: How did large-scale municipal housing projects like the Hufeisensiedlung demonstrate the social welfare priorities of Weimar local governments?

sources.lesson_title: KT1.4: Changes in Society, 1924–1929
sources.artifact_title: Right-Wing DNVP Campaign Emblem and Anti-Modernism Poster
sources.creator: Deutschnationale Volkspartei (DNVP) Campaign Bureau
sources.repository: Deutsches Historisches Museum (DHM), Berlin
sources.rights_status: Educational Fair Dealing / CDPA 1988 s.32 & Historical Election Poster
sources.caption: German National People's Party (DNVP) campaign insignia from the 1928 Reichstag election, rallying conservative Christians and nationalists against "Cultural Bolshevism", modern art, and American jazz.
sources.hinge_question: Why did right-wing traditionalists label modern architecture, jazz, and female independence as "Cultural Bolshevism"?

sources.hinge_question: How does the publication of vernacular botanical and herbal treatises demonstrate the broadening intellectual curiosity of Elizabethan gentry?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Thomas Harman’s Caveat for Common Cursitors (1567)
sources.creator: Thomas Harman / William Gryffith
sources.repository: British Library, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Title woodcut of Thomas Harman's 1567 pamphlet 'A Caveat or Warning for Common Cursitors', exposing the tricks and canting language of vagabonds.
sources.hinge_question: Why did Thomas Harman publish detailed classifications of rogues and vagabonds like 'Abraham Men' and 'Counterfeit Cranks'?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: The Elizabethan Poor Law Statute of 1601 (Parliamentary Roll)
sources.creator: Parliament of England
sources.repository: Parliamentary Archives, London
sources.rights_status: Crown Copyright / Open Parliament Licence / Public Domain
sources.caption: The official parchment statute of the 1601 Act for the Relief of the Poor (43 Elizabeth I c. 2), codifying Elizabethan poor relief into permanent law.
sources.hinge_question: How did the 1601 Poor Law create a formal national system that distinguished between the 'deserving' and 'undeserving' poor?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Contemporary Woodcut of Vagrants Punished in Stocks and at the Cart-Tail
sources.creator: Tudor Broadside Illustrator
sources.repository: British Library, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sixteenth-century woodcut illustrating the public punishment of vagrants: tied to the end of a cart and stripped to the waist to be flogged.
sources.hinge_question: What does the severity of corporal punishments in Tudor woodcuts reveal about Elizabethan fears of social disorder and roving gangs?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: William Cecil's Parliamentary Memoranda on Grain Inflation and Enclosure (1570s)
sources.creator: Sir William Cecil (State Papers)
sources.repository: The National Archives, Kew
sources.rights_status: Open Government Licence / Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir William Cecil, who recognized that population growth, debasement of coinage, and sheep enclosure caused devastating grain price inflation and rural unemployment.
sources.hinge_question: How do Cecil's private notes show that ministers recognized economic factors like poor harvests and enclosure drove rural poverty?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.2: The Problem of the Poor and Vagrancy, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Quarter Sessions Records of Justices of the Peace in Norfolk
sources.creator: Clerk of the Peace, Norfolk
sources.repository: Norfolk Record Office, Norwich
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Norfolk county magistrate records documenting the appointment of searchers to apprehend masterless men and supervise parish work schemes.
sources.hinge_question: How do local magistrates' court records corroborate the claim that vagrancy laws were enforced unevenly across different English counties?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: English Naval Galleons with Low-Profile Race-Built Hulls (c. 1585)
sources.creator: Naval Architectural Draftsman
sources.repository: National Maritime Museum, Greenwich
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Naval engraving showing the design of John Hawkins' innovative race-built galleons: lower forecastles, streamlined keels, and heavier broadside guns.
sources.hinge_question: How did John Hawkins' race-built galleons give English navigators decisive technical advantages in speed and weatherly sailing?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Sir Francis Drake with Navigational Compass and Terrestrial Globe
sources.creator: Jodocus Hondius
sources.repository: National Portrait Gallery, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Portrait of Sir Francis Drake holding a mariner's compass beside an open terrestrial globe, painted by Jodocus Hondius c. 1583.
sources.hinge_question: How does Drake's deliberate inclusion of the compass and globe promote England's ambition to rival the Spanish Empire globally?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Augustine Ryther's Sea Chart of the English Channel and Atlantic Approaches
sources.creator: Augustine Ryther
sources.repository: National Maritime Museum, Greenwich
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Engraved maritime chart by Augustine Ryther (1590) displaying coastal soundings, compass roses, and latitude lines along the Atlantic seaboard.
sources.hinge_question: What does this navigational chart indicate about the growing cartographic accuracy available to late Elizabethan ship captains?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Sir John Hawkins, Treasurer of the Royal Navy and Slave Trade Pioneer
sources.creator: West Country Artist
sources.repository: The Box, Plymouth City Museum
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir John Hawkins, who led three transatlantic slave-trading voyages between 1562 and 1568, backed secretly by Queen Elizabeth and London syndicates.
sources.hinge_question: How did Hawkins' early triangular slave trade voyages in the 1560s establish the commercial and naval foundations of English oceanic expansion?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.3: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery, 1558–1588
sources.artifact_title: Sir Richard Grenville, Vice-Admiral and Commander of the 1585 Virginia Expedition
sources.creator: Unknown English Artist
sources.repository: National Portrait Gallery, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Richard Grenville (1542–1591), fierce naval commander who transported the first English colonists to Roanoke Island in 1585 in the Tiger.
sources.hinge_question: How does Grenville's dual career as a naval combatant and colonial commander reflect the militarized nature of Elizabethan maritime expansion?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: Sir Walter Raleigh, Courtier, Explorer, and Coloniser (c. 1588)
sources.creator: Nicholas Hilliard or Workshop
sources.repository: National Portrait Gallery, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Sir Walter Raleigh (1554–1618), royal favourite who received a royal patent from Elizabeth in 1584 granting him exclusive rights to colonize 'Virginia'.
sources.hinge_question: Why was Sir Walter Raleigh unable to lead the Virginia colonization expeditions in person despite holding the royal patent from Elizabeth?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: The Roanoke Island Colony Map by John White (1585)
sources.creator: John White
sources.repository: British Museum, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: John White's detailed watercolor map of the coast of Virginia and North Carolina from Cape Lookout to the Chesapeake Bay, surveyed in 1585.
sources.hinge_question: How does John White's detailed chart of the Outer Banks explain why treacherous shoals caused the flagship Tiger to run aground and ruin food supplies?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: John White Watercolor of an Algonquin Chief (Herowan) of Roanoke (1585)
sources.creator: John White
sources.repository: British Museum, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: John White's watercolor of a coastal Algonquin chief (herowan) adorned with copper ornaments, feathers, and body paint, painted from life in 1585.
sources.hinge_question: What does White's portrait of an indigenous leader reveal about initial English intentions to study and engage with local tribes?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: John White's Painting of an Algonquin Religious Feast and Dance at Secotan
sources.creator: John White
sources.repository: British Museum, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Watercolor by John White depicting a ritual circle dance of Algonquin priests and dancers with carved posts surrounding the sacred ceremonial ground at Secotan.
sources.hinge_question: How reliable is John White's artwork as primary ethnographical evidence of pre-colonial Native American culture?

sources.lesson_title: KT 3.4: Raleigh and the Colonisation of Virginia, 1584–1590
sources.artifact_title: John White Watercolor of an Algonquin Man and Woman Eating at Meat (1585)
sources.creator: John White
sources.repository: British Museum, London
sources.rights_status: Public Domain
sources.caption: Watercolor by John White showing an Algonquin couple seated on a reed mat eating a meal of boiled maize, fish, and tobacco.
sources.hinge_question: How does White's depiction of indigenous maize and dietary habits corroborate Thomas Harriot's written report on the agricultural potential of Virginia?
